questions.question: What are the Rules of Hooks and why do they exist?
questions.title: Rules Of Hooks
questions.direct_answer: Two rules: (1) Only call hooks at the top level — never inside conditions, loops, or nested functions. (2) Only call hooks from React functions (components or custom hooks), not plain functions. They exist because React identifies hooks BY CALL ORDER in a per-component slot list — conditional or reordered calls make the slots misalign between renders, and the wrong state lands in the wrong hook. The lint plugin (eslint-plugin-react-hooks) enforces both statically.

sections.title: Interview Answer
Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    R1[render 1: slot 1, 2, 3] --> R2[render 2: slot 1, 2, 3]
    R2 -->|same order| OK[state lands in the right hook]
    BAD{conditional hook?}
    BAD -->|render A| S1[slots: name, count, effect]
    BAD -->|render B| S2[slots: name, effect]
    S2 --> ERR[slot misalignment - crash]
    FIX[always call hooks + conditional return AFTER] --> STABLE
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
Why order-based identity (the design history): hooks store state in a linked list per fiber — each hook call appends and reads by position, because generating keys for anonymous hook calls (there's no name at the call site to key by — aliases, destructuring, wrapping in helpers all obscure identity) proved fragile. Call order is the one property stable across renders for top-level code. It's the same tradeoff as positional function arguments vs named — React chose positional and enforces the discipline with the lint rule.

The consequences worth being able to name (the depth markers): (1) a custom hook's hooks become part of the CALLER's slot sequence — a conditional custom hook breaks the caller just like a conditional useState; (2) hooks called dynamically by variadic patterns (useManyHooks(n)) are structurally impossible, not just discouraged; (3) the error messages ('Rendered more/fewer hooks than during the previous render') are slot-count mismatches — every production React developer has seen one, and knowing it means slot misalignment instantly.

The enforcement layer (the ecosystem answer): eslint-plugin-react-hooks' rules-of-hooks catches conditionals/loops/calls in non-React scopes at lint time, and exhaustive-deps analyzes effect dependencies — both enabled via the react-hooks config preset in create-react-app, Next.js, and Vite templates by default. The React Compiler (2024+) is the next layer: it understands hook semantics deeply enough to auto-memoize, and it validates rules compliance at build time. The one-line summary for the interview: the rules exist because hooks have no names — order IS their identity.
